Cobia (Rachycentron canadum) exhibit a life-history strategy typical of large, fast-growing pelagic predators. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, having completed the process of chorion rupture, initially weigh a mere 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams], a mass reflecting the modest energy reserves contained within the 1.4 mm diameter egg. This lecithotrophic stage is brief, as the embryo's endogenous yolk is rapidly depleted. The progression from egg hatching to the onset of first exogenous feeding is temperature-dependent; under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 12.9 °C [T = 12.9 °C], the estimated age at birth is 4.55 days [ab = 4.55 days]. This rapid transition from an endotrophic to an exotrophic larval phase underscores the species' high early metabolic demands and its reliance on planktonic prey availability immediately following the point of no return.

As the free-swimming larva develops into a juvenile and progresses toward reproductive maturity, substantial variation in body size at puberty has been documented across different populations or cohorts. Some studies indicate that individuals may attain sexual maturity at a total length of 51.8 centimeters [Lp = 51.8 centimeters], a milestone that corresponds to a calculated wet weight at puberty of 1135 grams [Wwp = 1135 grams]. This relatively modest size at maturation likely reflects earlier reproduction under favorable environmental conditions or high population turnover. In contrast, other assessments based on growth curve modeling suggest that puberty is more commonly reached at a larger total length of 69.6 centimeters [Lp = 69.6 centimeters], which translates to a considerably greater body mass of 2.27 kilograms [Wwp = 2.27 kilograms]. The disparity between these two estimates may arise from geographic variation, differences in sampling methodology, or the application of distinct length-weight conversion factors.

The maximum recorded body size for this species is defined by an ultimate total length of 200 centimeters [Li = 200 centimeters], placing Rachycentron canadum among the largest members of the family Rachycentridae. Specimens approaching this asymptotic length achieve correspondingly massive body weights; the calculated ultimate wet weight for an individual of this size is 68.6 kilograms [Wwi = 68.6 kilograms], aligning closely with published records of the heaviest Cobia ever documented at approximately 68.0 kg. This considerable adult body mass, which allows the species to dominate pelagic food webs, is a product of a prolonged growth phase that continues well after the onset of reproduction. The species is relatively long-lived, with a maximum lifespan estimated at 15 years [am = 15 years] under the stable thermal regime of 12.9 °C [T = 12.9 °C]. This longevity, common among large coastal scombroids and carangids, allows for multiple reproductive seasons and contributes to the species' high lifetime reproductive output.

The reproductive potential of Cobia is extraordinarily high, a trait that compensates for substantial early-life mortality typical of pelagic spawners. At the reference temperature of 12.9 °C [T = 12.9 °C], females can achieve a remarkable maximum reproduction rate. This output can be deconstructed into its component parts: each spawning event yields approximately 1500 eggs per kilogram of body weight [N_R_i = approximately 1500 eggs per kilogram of body weight], and a single female may complete up to 10 spawning events per year [F_R_i = up to 10 spawning events per year] during the extended breeding season. The combination of high batch fecundity and frequent spawning results in an enormous yearly investment in offspring, reflecting a classic r-selected life-history component that is balanced by the species' large body size and relatively long lifespan.

Comparisons with related species within the order Carangiformes highlight the rapid growth and substantial size achieved by Cobia. While many jack species reach similar maximum lengths, few attain the same combination of mass at maturity and fecundity. In field surveys conducted at 12.9 °C [T = 12.9 °C], individuals attaining 51.8 cm [Lp = 51.8 cm] and 69.6 cm [Lp = 69.6 cm] at puberty are both found at sizes well below the asymptotic maximum length of 200 cm [Li = 200 cm], revealing a life history in which reproductive activity commences well before somatic growth is complete. The transition from a body mass of 1135 grams [Wwp = 1135 grams] or 2.27 kilograms [Wwp = 2.27 kilograms] at puberty to the ultimate body mass of 68.6 kilograms [Wwi = 68.6 kilograms] represents a prolonged period of post-maturational growth during which individuals accumulate substantial somatic tissue. Successful recruitment from the pelagic larval phase thus depends on matching high fecundity with favorable oceanographic conditions to ensure adequate feeding and growth.
